title: Rethink on 'safe harbour': Govt looks at scrapping legal immunity for social media platforms
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Soumyarendra Barik)
syllabus: GS3 › Challenges to internal security through communication networks; role of media and social networking sites · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; Parliament and legislation (IT Act) · GS4 › Ethics of technology; accountability
summary: The IT Ministry has begun discussing a proposal to withdraw 'safe harbour' (Section 79, IT Act) from social media platforms whose algorithms decide what users see, keeping it only for services that merely carry content.
evolution: To counter AI misinformation, invest in skills and literacy (misinformation thread).
ideas: A narrower shield: the government is exploring restricting safe harbour to services that merely transmit information (ISPs, telecom providers, peer-to-peer messaging) rather than social media that actively determine what users see.
GS3 · Regulation of intermediaries
India may limit safe harbour to mere carriers of content, ending blanket immunity for platforms that curate.
From carrier to curator: algorithms that boost engagement and virality mean platforms 'definitely determine what gets shown' and are no longer passive carriers.
GS3 · Social media
Once algorithms decide what millions see, a platform's role looks less like a postman and more like a publisher.

A business model at stake: safe harbour let Meta, Google and X build huge businesses on user content without a publisher's liability, so withdrawal could set up a major confrontation with tech companies and civil society.
GS3 · Digital economy
Safe harbour underpins the platform economy, so changing it affects innovation and investment, not only content.
Due process: immunity is conditional on due diligence, and stripping it would require amending the IT Act, 2000 through Parliament; talks are still exploratory.
GS2 · Legislation / rule of law
Any change to platform immunity must come through Parliament, with debate, not by executive notification alone.
Amplification without accountability: the core concern is that recommendation systems can shape public discourse while staying insulated from liability for what they amplify.
GS3 · Internal security (disinformation) / GS4 · Accountability
Platforms that profit from amplifying content must share responsibility for the harm that amplification causes.
keywords: Safe harbour
Legal protection shielding intermediaries from liability for third-party content (Section 79, IT Act)
GS3 · Cyber regulation
Safe harbour under Section 79 protects platforms only so long as they observe due diligence.
Mere conduit
A service that only transmits content without selecting or modifying it
GS3 · Intermediary liability
The proposal would keep immunity for mere conduits like telecom providers but not for curating platforms.
Algorithmic amplification
Recommendation systems pushing some content to more users for engagement
GS3 · Social media / disinformation
Algorithmic amplification, not the post itself, is what turns a falsehood into a public-order threat.
Chilling effect
When fear of liability makes speakers or platforms censor lawful content
GS2 · Article 19 / GS3
Removing immunity risks a chilling effect, as platforms may over-remove lawful speech to avoid liability.
Intermediary due diligence
Obligations platforms must meet to keep safe harbour
GS3 · Cyber regulation
Calibrated due diligence, scaled to a platform's reach, can ensure accountability without abolishing safe harbour.
examples: Conditional immunity for intermediaries, now under review
Section 79's safe harbour is the legal base of India's platform economy, and its review shows regulation catching up with algorithms.
IT Ministry summons Meta's global executives (July 2026)
Government examining how platforms decide reach and visibility
Summoning Meta's top policy executives shows India asserting regulatory sovereignty over global platforms.
pyqs: Fake news and disinformation as a threat to internal security; amendments to the IT Intermediary Guidelines.
Social media and encrypted messaging as security challenges; measures and remedies.
Use of internet and social media by non-state actors for subversive activities; guidelines.
Ethical dilemmas raised by social media in the digital age.

trend.t: Social media questions began with misuse by non-state actors and radicalisation (2015, 2016), moved to the security implications of social media and encrypted messaging (2024), and reached the regulatory framework itself: the IT Intermediary Guidelines and disinformation (2026). GS4 (2025) asked about the ethical dilemmas of social media.
trend.watch: Social media regulation was asked in 2024 and 2026 in GS3 and in 2025 in GS4, so it is a must-study area. Questions now ask about the rules for platforms, not just the threats.
focus: Intermediary liability: Section 79, IT Rules, due diligence

potential: Should social media platforms continue to enjoy 'safe harbour' protection for user content? Critically examine in the Indian context. (15 marks)
"Algorithms have turned social media platforms from carriers into curators of content." Discuss the implications for regulation in India. (10 marks)

practice.q: Should social media platforms continue to enjoy 'safe harbour' protection for user content? Critically examine in the Indian context.

answer.t: In November 2026 the IT Ministry began discussing withdrawing Section 79 safe harbour from social media platforms whose algorithms determine what users see.

pts.t: Without immunity, platforms may over-remove lawful posts to avoid liability, chilling speech under Article 19(1)(a).
pts.ex: Shreya Singhal (2015) required takedowns only on court or government order.

pts.t: Billions of posts cannot be checked in advance without heavy automated censorship.
Liability would favour only the largest firms that can afford compliance, hurting Indian startups.
User-generated content drives creators, small businesses and digital services.
pts.ex: Safe harbour let Meta, Google and X scale in India.

pts.t: Immunity already depends on due diligence and grievance redress under the IT Rules.
Wide liability can be used to pressure platforms against criticism.
Algorithms that push content for engagement make platforms active editors.
pts.ex: Government view: platforms 'no longer simple carriers'.

pts.t: Amplified fake news has triggered violence and threatens internal security.
Platforms earn from virality yet escape liability for its harms.
Harmful content reaches minors through recommendation feeds.
pts.ex: New York's law on chatbots and children (IE, 4 Nov 2026).

pts.t: Slow takedowns and opaque moderation frustrate victims.
Other jurisdictions now impose duties on very large platforms.
Duties scaled to a platform's size and reach rather than one rule for all.
Audits of recommendation systems and disclosure of how content is ranked.
Amend the IT Act after consultation, not by executive rules alone.
Reasoned orders and appeal to protect lawful speech.
An expert regulator rather than direct government control.

answer.t: Safe harbour should be narrowed, not abolished: platforms that amplify must be accountable, but speech must not become the casualty of that accountability.

title: How welfare board will function, what changes for unorganised, gig workers
where: Economy, page 10 (Ravi Dutta Mishra & Aanchal Magazine)
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Labour reforms · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections; Statutory bodies
summary: Follow-up: the Labour Ministry has notified two social security boards (40 members for unorganised workers, 22 for gig and platform workers) under the Code on Social Security.
evolution: Labour Ministry notifies the National Social Security Board under the Code on Social Security (Economy, page 23).
Details: two boards, aggregator contributions to a social security fund, and EPFO coverage widened.
ideas: Two boards, not one: a 40-member board for unorganised workers and a 22-member board for gig and platform workers, which includes aggregators such as quick-commerce and delivery platforms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
Separate boards recognise that gig and platform workers need schemes designed for platform work.
Who pays: aggregators must contribute 1–2% of annual turnover to a social security fund, capped at 5% of what they pay workers; the fund also draws on governments, CSR and fines.
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Aggregator contributions put part of the cost of gig workers' security on the platforms that profit from them.
What it covers: schemes for life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection and crèches.
GS2 · Welfare
Social security for gig workers spans life-cycle risks, from maternity to old age.
Wider formal coverage: EPFO provisions now apply to all establishments with 20 or more employees, regardless of industry, not only those in the old schedule.
GS3 · Labour reforms
Extending EPFO to all establishments with 20+ workers widens formal social security.
keywords: Social Security Fund
Pooled fund for unorganised, gig and platform workers
GS2 · Welfare
A dedicated Social Security Fund gives gig workers' schemes a stable financing base.
Aggregator levy
Platforms paying a share of turnover towards workers' welfare
GS3 · Labour
The aggregator levy shares the cost of social protection with platforms.
data: Aggregators' contribution to the social security fund, capped at 5% of amounts payable to workers
Code on Social Security, via IE
Aggregators must contribute 1–2% of turnover to gig workers' social security, capped at 5% of payouts (Code on Social Security).
examples: Aggregators on the gig workers' board
Platforms sit with worker bodies to design welfare schemes
GS2 · Tripartism, statutory bodies · GS3 · Digital economy
Putting aggregators and worker bodies on one board shows tripartism adapting to the platform economy.
pyqs: The gig economy and women's empowerment.
